The James Webb Space Telescope

By: Julian Sun | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The James Webb Space Telescope: Mankind's most powerful window of the universe

Unique Selling Point:
We reveal the first images of the James Webb Space Telescope. In July, NASA released the first images taken by the $10 Billion James Webb Space Telescope. Able to look back further in time than any telescope ever produced, the successor to the Hubble Space Telescope offered a tantalizing glimpse of its power and potential.

Summary:
The James Webb Space Telescope is the successor to Hubble. It was conceptualised back in the ’90s but has taken almost 30 years and $10 Billion to build. After years of planning, it finally launched into space on the 31st of December 2021. About as half as big as a 737 aircraft and with a space shield the size of a telescope, it is an engineering marvel. Last week NASA released the very first images revealing the universe as we’ve never seen it before. These 5 images offer a tantalising glimpse into the potential of WebbWe will also compare and contrast the power of the JWST by visiting the South African Large Telescope (SALT) in Sutherland - South Africa’s most powerful optical telescope

Press Release:


Why are we here? Are we alone? How did it all begin? Last Christmas the James Webb Space Telescope was launched into space on a 10-year mission to help find those answers. The size of a school bus, Webb is the successor to the legendary Hubble Space Telescope. Six times larger and a hundred times more powerful, its infrared view of the universe has already heralded the most exquisite pictures of the earliest galaxies and the birth and death of stars. Carte Blanche gets lost in these first stunning images of colliding galaxies and exoplanets with atmospheres that, tantalisingly, could sustain life.

Script:


JAMES WEBB SPACE TELESCOPE: SCRIPT

INTRO
Claire is staring up into the night sky using a sky-map app to visualise the Milky Way Galaxy

Close-up shot of iPhone showing the Milky Way

CLAIRE: They say that there are more stars in the universe than there are grains of sand on all the beaches on planet Earth. It’s enough to make you feel infinitesimally small and wonder about our place in the universe.
B-roll Montage of fantastic images from Hubble, time-lapses from S.A.A.O
CLAIRE VOICE OVER:
Are we alone? How did it all begin? These are the deepest of questions. Throughout history, humans have looked up to the stars for the answers, first with our eyes and then with telescopes. For over 400 years they have provided views of distant galaxies with ever-increasing detail.
It’s an exciting time for astronomy as breathtaking advances in technology are allowing us to see deeper into space than ever before.
One example can be found in Sutherland in the Northern Cape, the best place to view the stars in South Africa.

S.A.L.T - SUTHERLAND
CLAIRE: This is the massive mirror of the South African Large Telescope. It’s only when you get this close to it that you understand the scale of the most powerful optical telescope in the Southern Hemisphere
CLAIRE VOICE OVER: Dr Moses Mogotsi is a resident astronomer at SALT
Wide-establishing shot of Claire and Moses
DR MOSES MOGOTSI: When technology came along to build telescopes such as what Galileo Galilei did, it opened up a whole new world because now we could see these little tiny dots in the sky as more than just that. For example, when you look at something like Jupiter, it goes from just being a bright light in the night sky to being a planet with moons, which is very, very exciting to begin with. And the technology developed further and further So. And now we're building massive telescopes on the earth and also big telescopes that we’re sending up into space and observing all sorts of different kinds of light with these telescopes.
CLAIRE: What is some of the work that is done here at Salt?
DR MOSES MOGOTSI: So a lot of I guess the astronomy work that we do is we observe all sorts of different kinds of objects in the sky, from stars to galaxies to asteroids. And the South African large telescope has all this capability to do all sorts of different kinds of interesting science looking at these kinds of objects
We see climbing onto the platform as the giant SALT rotates
CLAIRE VOICE OVER: The 11x9m mirror of SALT is so big because it has to see through the Earth’s atmosphere
DR MOSES MOGOTSI [00:08:28] When you're on the ground, we have the atmosphere and the atmosphere is great. It allows us to breathe. We don't die of skin cancer, a lot of very useful things. Atmosphere. That's right. But the problem is it can also affect the images that we see. So it's so much better than when you can have a telescope that is outside of the atmosphere. because then it means a telescope that is smaller than ours can just see so much more in terms of see things in better detail and see more distant things

THE JAMES WEBB SPACE TELESCOPE
CLAIRE VOICE OVER: Last Christmas saw the launch of the most complex ever: The $10 billion James Webb Space Telescope.

LAUNCH CONTROL: Lift off from a tropical rain forest to the edge of time itself, James Webb begins a voyage back to the birth of the universe
CLAIRE VOICE OVER: NASA’s Dr Begonia Villa is a systems engineer on Webb
DR BEGONA VILLA Webb is the largest and most complex observatory that we have launched into space up till now. I am in charge of two of the instruments on Webb, one of them on the guidance sensor that keeps the observatory pointing and very stable.
[00:10:31] The launch was perfect, it was the best Christmas present we could have had and the launch was perfect. I think any launch is a special event, but particularly when you see I think we all saw this our child and we are letting it go. I was lucky to be in French Guiana at the launch site. So it was super wonderful to be there and a wonderful experience.
CLAIRE: [00:07:49] What were the Webb's objectives?
DR BEGONA VILA: [00:01:18] This telescope has taken, like many of these big observatories many years to come to fruition, almost 25 years since the first concept was designed. The request was to have a telescope that could look back in time to the first galaxies and the stars that formed in the universe, to keep looking for formation of the stars and planets around them. That's important because it's helping us to search for the answer if we are alone. Right, how many other planets will have the possibility of life?

THE SUCCESSOR TO HUBBLE
CLAIRE VOICE OVER: Webb is the successor to the iconic Hubble Space Telescope. For over 3 decades, it has revealed some of the most spectacular images of the universe. Much like our eyes, Hubble sees primarily visible light but this has its limitations.
To study the early universe, Webb has been designed to see infrared light.

This is because since the Big Bang, the universe has been expanding which means that everything is moving further away from us

This causes light from distant objects to be get stretched from the optical to the infrared, which is invisible to Hubble but not to Webb.

Dr Rosalind Skelton is an astronomer from the South African Astronomical Observatory.

DR ROSALIND SKELTON So looking with James Webb, particularly, we can look back to those early phases of the universe when galaxies were just a few hundred million years old, that just started forming and that light has then travelled towards us for billions of years since then. When we're looking at these distant galaxies and stars, we seeing that object as it was when the light was emitted, even if that light was emitted millions or billions of years ago.

CLAIRE: [00:04:44] Wow. So we could be looking at things that are no longer there?
DR ROSALIND SKELTON [00:04:47] Definitely!

UNFOLDING WEBB
We see an animation of the Webb being unfolded in space
CLAIRE VOICE OVER: Unlike Hubble, which orbits the Earth, Webb orbits the sun, 1.5 million KM away from our planet. The Earth helps to block out heat from the sun as the telescope needs to be kept at -230 degrees centigrade to operate properly. That’s why Webb has been fitted with a sun-shield, the size of a tennis court to act as a giant beach umbrella.

DR BEGONA VILA: We can think about the infra-red as heat. Everything emits heat. So we’re are trying to get the heat, the signal of these very faint objects we are looking at. We need to cool everything else down.

CLAIRE VOICE OVER: The centrepiece of Webb is the 6.5m gold-plated mirror. Gold improves the mirror’s reflection of infrared light.
DR BEGONA VILA: It doesn't fit inside the rocket, so it's made of 18 smaller mirrors that we can fold down and then open when we are in space.
CLAIRE VOICE OVER: Once unfolded, engineers on the ground had to precisely align the mirrors remotely. To do this Webb focused on a star. At first, it produced 18 separate images. For the next 2 months, the mirrors were painstakingly adjusted until they formed one single mirror and one perfectly focused star. Finally in July, the first breathtaking images from Webb were released to the world




WEBB’S FIRST IMAGES
Claire and Moses look through the images from Webb with the help of an iPad

CLAIRE: [00:14:12] Okay, so take me through some of these images. What am I looking at here? Because I'm just seeing a pretty picture.
THE WEBB DEEP FIELD
DR MOSES MOGOTSI [00:14:18] I'm also seeing a pretty picture, but the pretty picture is incredible in that first thing that you notice, you obviously a very beautiful look at the quality of like images we're seeing here. But what's happening is you have these galaxies over here and they're kind of sitting in the front and they're so massive that they're causing the light from galaxies behind them to be bent around. And when that light is bent around, it causes something that's called lensing. And lensing results in these streaks that we see here on the sides of these arcs that we see over here. These are actually this is light from galaxies that are very much more distant than these ones, but it's being bent because of how much matter is there.

CLAIRE: [00:00:18] when I'm looking at this, could you maybe give me an example of the scope or the scale of what I am seeing in the sky? When I look at this image. [00:00:28][9.2]
DR MOSES MOGOTSI [00:00:28] So if you're looking at this, it may not look like this when you look at it, but this is a tiny part of the sky. So I was like a grain of like rice or something like that. Tiny, tiny, tiny part of the sky just sitting up there

THE COSMIC CLIFF: CARINA’S NEBULA
CLAIRE: [00:00:58] Blowing my mind. Okay. Let's look at something else then. This is another pretty picture I saw, and I did not know what I was looking at.

DR MOSES MOGOTSI [00:01:06] So this is what we call a nebula. And it's a star-forming region. So when you look at this region over here, there are young stars that are being born in those clouds. Optical light, it's difficult for it to get through things like dust. So when we have areas like this that have a lot of matter and a lot of like dust in the way, when you're looking at in optical, sometimes it could be difficult to see through it and with James Webb, because it can look at it in Infra- Red, you can see deeper into it than you could have optical. So we've seen level of detail and more objects in here when we could in the optical
CLAIRE: [00:02:29] What you see, I know your voice when I was looking at the pictures the first time. That's incredible!

WASP-96B - EXOPLANET
CLAIRE VOICE OVER: There is a connection between Webb and the observatory here in Sutherland
DR ROSALIND SKELTON [00:11:29] one of the first images of James Webb was of the exoplanet atmosphere. That exoplanet was discovered in Sutherland. So using one of our small telescopes called WASP WASP South, that's the telescope that found this planet, WASP 96B.
CLAIRE VOICE OVER: Discovered in Sutherland in 2013, Wasp96B is a gas giant like Jupiter. It orbits a star over 1000 light years away from Earth. Almost a decade after its discovery, Webb was able to analyze its atmosphere
DR MOSES MOGOTSI [00:10:52] So one of the cool things of the spectrum is that we're looking at an exoplanet and be able to study its atmosphere. Wow. Which is like incredible right now in the spectrum we're seeing, oh, look, there's some signatures of water in the atmosphere of the planet. So think we are able to now observe these other exoplanets and sometimes be able to detect water in the atmosphere as it gets closer and closer to being able to actually find life on other planets, which is super exciting.

OUTRO
DR BEGONA VILA [00:36:05] So when we say it’s going to rewrite the history books in astronomy, that is totally true.
CLAIRE VOICE OVER: From stellar nurseries from which new stars are born, to ethereal photos capturing their death, to distant galaxies colliding, these tantalizing first images from Webb are just a taste of things to come. With a lifespan of at least 10 years, we can look forward to many more as we continue to explore the wonders of our universe.







PROMO 2:
CLAIRE: From Galileo to Hubble, man has used telescopes to study the stars for centuries.
Moses: [00:00:32] this is a tiny part of the sky, it's probably like a grain of like rice,if you would look at it, you think, oh, there's probably nothing there, yet, looking at it with such a telescope, you can see so, so much
CLAIRE: Now the James Webb Space Telescope will allow us to see closer than ever before.


PROMO 3:
CLAIRE: In July, NASA released the first images from the $10 billion James Webb Space Telescope
Moses: [00:01:18] if we looked deep inside those clouds, some of them would have young stars that are literally being born.
CLAIRE: It’s a tantalizing glimpse of the potential of the most complex observatory ever launched into space.
